heading: What the host adds
body:
The host adds three things. First, `data-platform="native"` on the document body. With it, a page can behave differently without checking the user agent string (the text that names the browser). Second, the list of window controls that the manifest granted, and nothing else. A service reaches them through the injected `WindowControls` browser API. Third, the service channel, which works in both directions.

On macOS, the host also builds the standard menu bar, with the items that `tac.application.menus` declares. On Linux and Windows, it shows a menu bar with File, Edit and Window menus and the declared items (see Native menus). A menu item opens a page or calls a service method; it gives the page no new capability. These three desktop hosts also run application services: Rust services with `#[Lifetime({"value":"application"})]` that start with the app and stop when it quits.

On macOS, `"titleBar": "integrated"` in `tac.application.window` lets the page reach the top edge of the window. The host then sets the CSS custom properties `--tac-titlebar-height`, `--tac-titlebar-leading-inset` and `--tac-titlebar-trailing-inset`, and it moves the window when a person drags an element marked `data-tac-drag-region` (see Window controls). This is a window setting, not a new capability.

On purpose, Tachyon adds no other capability vocabulary (a fixed list of platform actions). A compiled service can use its platform's SDK because it was compiled in that language for that target. A list of verbs between them would contain only the part that Tachyon had built.
